name: ospren
author: rule-family designer (world: a 5x5 picture of black and white squares)
description: 5x5-PICTURE RULE-FAMILY class (docs/RULE_FAMILIES.md; brainstorm in challenges/lab/NOTES_rules_pixels.md). CLUE = 2 or 3 example pictures, five lines of five characters from '#' (black) and '.' (white), separated by a blank line, ALL WITH DIFFERENT NUMBERS OF BLACK SQUARES and pairwise at least 3 squares apart. ANSWER = one more 5x5 picture obeying the hidden rule, with 2..15 black squares, using a NUMBER OF BLACK SQUARES THAT IS NOT IN THE CLUE and differing from every example in AT LEAST TWO SQUARES. Those two well-formedness clauses are the design decision that made the class (see below); the first is visible in the clue itself because the examples never share a count. UNIVERSE U: 10 templates, 29 rules; the scorer reduces a picture to a 15-number readout (blacks; same in a left-right mirror; same flipped top-to-bottom; same turned upside down; black corners; rows used; columns used; blobs of squares joined side by side; completely black rows; completely black columns; middle square black; every row the same number; every column the same number; biggest blob; black squares standing alone) and every rule is one readout number equal to one constant. COUNT exactly n blacks, n=5,6,7; SYM mirror / top-bottom flip / half turn; CORNERS exactly n of the four corners black, n=1..4; SPREAD the blacks sit in exactly n rows or n columns, n=1,2; BLOBS exactly n blobs, n=1..4 (n=1 = all joined up in one blob); FULLLINE exactly one row / exactly one column completely black; MIDDLE the middle square is black; EQLINE every row / every column has the same number of blacks; MAXBLOB the biggest blob is n squares, n=2,3,4; LONELY exactly n black squares stand completely alone, n=3,4,5. Only 21 of the 29 may be the HIDDEN rule: a rule is eligible only if a naive random picture (count uniform in 2..15, then that many random squares) satisfies it with probability <= 0.20 - that number is what a player who answers at random scores. The other 8 - the three COUNT rules, 1 and 2 black corners, 3 and 4 blobs, and 'the middle square is black' - stay in U as COMPETITORS the generator has to kill, which forces the clue's layout for free: the COUNT rules can only die if the examples disagree about the number of blacks (which is exactly the convention the answer's fresh-count clause needs), MIDDLE can only die if some example has a white middle and another a black one, and the loose CORNERS/BLOBS parameters stop the clue from being three pictures that look alike. Mean density of the hidden rule under a random picture: 0.070. GENERATE draws the TEMPLATE uniformly and only then a parameter (so no idea of the class is rare merely for owning fewer rules), then one example per black-count from a precomputed 11000-picture pool, and keeps the set only if the examples together leave exactly one rule of U alive while no proper subset does (uniqueness + minimality). Measured over 500 clues: 500/500 unique, 500/500 minimal, 500/500 distinct counts, 500/500 examples >= 3 squares apart; 52% two examples, 48% three; template mix 53-73 of 500 each; generate 0.30 ms mean (the pool and its 29-bit per-picture rule masks are built at module level, 460 ms once per worker, not charged to max_generate_ms); clue <= 91 chars; answer 29 chars. U IS AN ANTICHAIN (0 nesting violations over the pool), otherwise positive examples could never separate two rules; that is why 'as many blacks above the middle row as below' is absent (it is implied by BOTH top-bottom symmetry and 'every row the same number'), why 'the top row is the same as the bottom row' is absent (implied by the top-bottom flip), why 'the four corners are all the same colour' is absent (it contains the 0-corner and 4-corner rules), why MAXBLOB starts at 2 ('the biggest blob is 1' IS 'no two blacks touch', which is dense), and why 'the black squares make a straight line' is absent (it contains 'all the blacks are in one row'). The 2..15 cap on the number of blacks exists to kill the all-black picture, which satisfies seven eligible rules at once (all three symmetries, 4 corners, 1 blob, equal rows, equal columns) and would have been a 30% constant answer with no insight. A rule that FIXES the number of blacks can never be pinned under the fresh-count clause, so 'every row has exactly one black square' is impossible here - the survivor of that family is 'every row has the SAME number'. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED (never in U, frequently consistent with the examples - learning what this class never says is the game; 'fits' = consistent with every example, 'scores' = a player who always answers a well-formed instance of it): 'every square that is black in ALL the examples is black' (what do they have in common?) fits 100% scores 19%; 'at least n blacks (the clue's smallest)' fits 100% scores 10%; 'at most n blacks (the clue's biggest)' fits 100% scores 10%; 'the same number of blacks as an example' fits 100% scores 0% (the well-formedness clause makes it actively wrong - the cheapest lesson in the class); 'there is a black in the middle column' fits 58% scores 10%; 'the middle square is white' fits 36% scores 10%; 'every row has at least one black' fits 27% scores 10%; 'as many blacks above the middle row as below' fits 26% scores 12%; 'as many blacks left of the middle column as right' fits 23% scores 11%; 'the four corners are all the same colour' fits 18% scores 10%; 'the top row is the same as the bottom row' fits 11% scores 14%; 'the first column is the same as the last' fits 10% scores 13%; 'the top row is all white' fits 4% scores 12%; 'no two black squares touch' (the most obvious Zendo rule of all) fits only 1% scores 9% - a strong every-square property is a weak discriminator, so minimal example sets are almost never made of such pictures. The class only ever makes TIGHT statements about BLACK squares (exactly n corners, the biggest blob IS 4, EVERY row the SAME number, the picture IS its own mirror) and never loose ones (at least, at most, no two touching, there is a..., the top row is white); its strongest traps are the loose cousins of its own templates. On average 6.2 of the 14 exclusions are consistent with every example (never fewer than 4), so a player whose universe is U plus the obvious extras always faces several survivors: picking a random one scores 25%, picking a wrong one 11%, picking the true one 100%. WITNESSES over 500 fresh clues: copy an example verbatim 0%; one square flipped 0%; one black added 0%; one black rubbed out 0%; mirrored 0%; flipped top-bottom 0%; turned upside down 0%; transposed 0% (the count clause kills all four symmetries at once because they preserve the count; the two-square clause kills the three one-square edits); two squares flipped 13% (the cheapest legal probe - the foothold); a symmetric one-blob picture at a fresh count 19%; always a 2-blob picture ignoring the examples 13%; a random well-formed picture at a fresh count 8%, at any count 6%; a player who has mapped U perfectly 100%; U minus its two rarest templates 74-78%; the true rule 100%. SOLVE re-derives the survivor exactly as the scorer does and rejection-samples a random valid picture from a nine-way mixture of picture shapes at a random unused count (never canonical, never minimal). SCORE is 1004 chars (needs max_score_code_chars = 1024, the raise RULE_FAMILIES.md sec.4 allows for this paradigm): it parses the examples, computes the 15-number readout of each, rebuilds all 29 rules of U from a 58-character table, filters, insists on a single survivor and checks the answer is well formed, fresh and obedient. No hidden channel. Junk ('', '0', 'x', '1'*100, the clue itself, 4000 '#') scores 0 in under 0.005 ms without raising; the answer is parsed with split() so any line ending, trailing spaces or a one-line space-separated picture is accepted.
